title: The tiger who thought he was a goat
hook: a tiger cub raised by goats eats grass and bleats, until another tiger shows him the water
carry: know yourself free, and you are free

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashtavakra's bold answer. You are the witness, free right now. Today, the last day of jnana, and of the three paths.

Ramakrishna, the nineteenth-century saint of Bengal, told this one. A tigress leaps on a flock of goats, gives birth as she springs, and dies. Her cub grows up among the goats. It eats grass. It bleats. When danger comes, it runs with the herd. Years later, a wild tiger attacks the same flock and stops, astonished. A tiger, eating grass? It drags the young one to a pond. Look at your face in the water. It's just like mine. It gives him a taste of meat. And slowly, the tiger who thought he was a goat lets out a roar.
screen: `A TIGER RAISED BY GOATS.` → `A TIGER, EATING GRASS?` → `LOOK IN THE WATER. THE ROAR.`

segments.voice: The young tiger was never a goat. He was bound by what he took himself to be. In Ramakrishna's telling, the wild tiger is like the teacher, holding up the water. The Ashtavakra Gita says it in its first chapter. Paraphrased: whoever takes themselves to be free is free, and whoever takes themselves to be bound is bound. And it adds: the popular saying is true, as you think, so you become. Ya matih sa gatih. This isn't positive thinking. It's about identity, the heart of jnana. In Vedanta's reading, the atman, your real self, is already free, and bondage is mistaking yourself for the body, the job, the moods. Lose a job, and you can feel finished, because you took yourself to be the job. Jnana would say: that's the goat talking. Look in the water. That's the end of our jnana week: neti neti, the tenth man, Maitreyi, the lane in Kashi, Ashtavakra, and today the tiger at the pond. It's also the end of three weeks on the three paths. Karma: offer the work. Bhakti: love as the road. Jnana: know who you are. Some teachers see separate roads for the doer, the lover, the thinker. Vivekananda did, and added a fourth, raja yoga, the path of meditation. Others point to the Gita, which weaves all three through its chapters. Next: the school that says not two.
screen: `HE WAS NEVER A GOAT.` · `FREE IF YOU TAKE YOURSELF AS FREE.` · `THAT'S THE GOAT TALKING.` · `KARMA. BHAKTI. JNANA.` · then, large: `KNOW YOURSELF FREE.`

segments.voice: Try the three paths in one sitting: for karma, think of one piece of work waiting for you, and offer it; for bhakti, bring to mind someone or something you love, and let that love be there. Then, for jnana, ask quietly who is offering, who is loving, and don't answer; just rest as the one who's asking. If a sense of freedom comes, let it; if it doesn't, that's fine too.
Jnana yoga, the path of knowledge: knowing yourself as the free witness. Today's verse: whoever takes themselves as free is free. As you think, so you become.
Your line: know yourself free, and you are free. The tiger was a tiger all along. And that's the three paths, walked.

howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers present karma, bhakti and jnana (often with raja yoga, meditation) as paths suited to different temperaments, while also teaching that they support one another; parables like Ramakrishna's tiger raised among goats are used to show that the self is already free and only has to be recognized.

original.note: Sanskrit: 'as the mind, so the destination' — the saying quoted in Ashtavakra Gita 1.11.

trapdoor: what you thought: as you think, so you become is a self-help slogan.
what it means: in the Ashtavakra Gita, it's about what you take yourself to be: bound, or the free witness.
what a scholar hears: Ashtavakra Gita 1.11 calls it a true popular saying (kimvadantīha satyeyam); the idea that one's final thought shapes one's destination also appears in the Gita (8.6).
